paper_title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

sections.content: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp 1. Introduction Deployed image classifiers often need small, specific changes: fine-grained concept has to move to another class, recurring confusion between two classes has to be repaired, or rare subgroup is misclassified. Collecting data and finetuning is costly and can change behavior far beyond the requested fix. Model editing methods instead compute targeted weight change for one request [22, 24, 31]. Recently, general-purpose large language models (LLMs) have begun to edit networks directly, practice called weight-space programming [39]. Here, an LLM agent inspects activations and weights, finds the units that respond to concept, writes targeted change and checks its effect with forward passes, all without gradient descent. The networks such agents edit are, however, trained for accuracy alone. Nothing in their training asks that concept be represented in form that short, targeted edit can isolate. It is therefore unknown how well LLM agents edit standard vision models, and whether training can make networks easier for them to edit. We study both questions for image classification (see Fig. 1). Blinded LLM agents receive an edit request with few support images, edit any weight of the network through tool interface, without gradients, under fixed budget of forward passes, weight reads and weight edits, and are scored on held-out test images for success and side effects. During these edit processes, they relabel fine-grained concept, fix confusion between two classes, or fix misclassified subgroup, on Waterbirds [30], CIFAR-100 [19], PACS [20] and Entity-30 [32], with ResNet-18, ResNet-50 [12] and ViT-B/16 [6] classifiers. Five LLMs act as editors, led by GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, to edit networks that are trained in four ways: standard empirical risk minimization (ERM), label smoothing (LS), gradient-based editable training (ENN) [36], and Edit-Ready Training (ERT), which we introduce. Our pre-study revealed that agents mostly change the classifier head along the contrast between support and other images, and ERT rehearses such edits during training, so that the features become easy to edit this way. On four of the nine tested settings formed by dataset, task and backbone, standard networks are already easy to edit, and dedicated training adds little on average. Where they are hard to edit, ERT helps substantially for both main editors. On the Entity-30 confusion fix it raises the net score from 0.46 to 0.79 for Astra and from 0.44 to 0.74 for Opus, and on Waterbirds with ViT-B/16 from 0.50 to 0.74 and from 0.33 to 0.76. While none of the compared training methods is best across the board, ERT has the highest mean net score for both leading editors. Thus, our main contributions are as follows: We present systematic study of how well LLM agents edit trained vision classifiers, and how the classifier training affects edit quality. We propose Edit-Ready Training (ERT), which delivers the highest mean net edit score for GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 among all tested baselines. 1 Figure 1. Training vision models for weight-space programming. (a) Edit-Ready Training (ERT) simulates edits during training to make vision models better editable by LLMs. (b) Through our WeightLab an LLM agent can iteratively edit vision models weights to change its behavior. (c) ERT improves vision model editability through LLMs, which is indicated by an increased mean net edit score over all nine settings, and the gain of ERT over ERM on the three settings that are hardest (bars: 95% bootstrap confidence; : < 0.05). We release vision weight-space programming benchmark, alongside more than 75,000 logged tool calls describing scored edits from five LLM editors. 2. Related Work Weight-space analysis. Weight-space analysis treats the weights of trained networks as data. Test accuracy or training hyperparameters can be predicted from the weights alone [7, 40], representations learned on model zoos capture model characteristics without labels [33, 34], architectures for learning on weights respect the permutation symmetries of neurons [26, 42], and hypernetworks generate weights [11]. Interpretability research can assist the analysis of networks by assigning visual concepts to units [2], combining weights between units into circuits [28], and by describing units in natural language [13, 27]. Language models have recently taken over parts of this analysis. Agents with interpretability tools run experiments on vision models and explain their units [35], and language models have been trained to read weights [16]. Frontier LLMs identify small networks from their raw weights without such training [39], although their readings of small image networks break under label permutation [1]. Neural network editing. Network editing changes the behavior of trained network on specific input or concept while leaving the rest intact. Most methods compute the weight change with an algorithm: fine-tuning, learned hypernetworks that turn gradient into an edit [4, 24], or closedform low-rank updates at located layers [22, 23]. In vision, prediction rules are rewritten at chosen layer of classifier [31] or generative model [3], and concepts are erased from diffusion models [10]. Task arithmetic adds and subtracts weight differences [15], linear projections remove concept direction from the features [29], and retraining only the last layer corrects reliance on spurious features [17], which makes the classifier natural place for small edits. Weight-space programming [39] replaces the editing algorithm with an LLM that decides itself what to inspect and what to write. This offloads editing to LLM agents that carry out technical work autonomously [14]. Existing work [39] judges an edit only by its effect on the target behavior. Our benchmark also scores side effects and accuracy cost on heldout images, blinds the agent to the origin of the network, and compares several agents under one protocol. Few works target editability during training. Editable Neural Networks (ENN) [36] meta-train network, in the spirit of MAML [8], so that few gradient steps on new examples correct its predictions without harming others. We keep this structure but rehearse the edits that LLM agents perform. Apart from dedicated techniques, ordinary training choices also affect editability [21]. Label smoothing [25, 38] produces less extreme logits, and sparse final layers make classifier easier to inspect and debug [41]. To our knowledge, none of these methods has been evaluated with LLM editors. 3. Method Our approach has two parts, as shown in Fig. 1. First, EditReady Training (ERT) prepares network for later edits, by simulating head weight edits, computing the errors of the edited network, and backpropagating them through the edit into all weights. Second, Iterative Weight-Space Programming (WSP) edits the trained network afterwards in an iterative process. An LLM receives an edit request and few images, and uses our WeightLab sandbox server to 2 inspect the network, modify its native weights and check the result. We describe WSP first, because the rules of its editing protocol determine which edits ERT performs during training. 3.1. Iterative Weight-Space Programming To systematically investigate weight-space programming of vision models, an LLM edits trained network through WeightLab, our sandbox environment that exposes the network and enforces fixed editing protocol (Fig. 1, center). The protocol serves five purposes. It keeps the edits direct, such that the agent has no gradients, cannot train the network and cannot add layers or adapters, so it cannot fall back on fine-tuning, which would make it gradient-based editor. It further makes editors and training methods comparable, as every editor uses the same tools, budget and system prompt (Sec. A). Blinding keeps an editor from recognizing how network was trained. We record every edit by logging all calls and changes, which makes the edits analyzable (see Sec. 5.3). Finally, budget limits trial and error on the few support images, which would otherwise lead to overfitting. For our setup, we consider classifier with backbone that computes features (x) Rd and linear head with weights and bias b, so that the logits are z(x) = (x) + b. An edit request asks to move concept s, currently assigned to class y, to target class t, while all other predictions stay as they are. More generally, an edit request consists of few support images labeled with the class they should receive and set of reference images labeled with the networks current predictions, which should not change. Besides relabeling concept, we consider two kinds of requests that correct existing errors: fixing confusion, where images of one class are predicted as another class, and fixing subgroup, where images of one class from particular domain, such as sketches, are misclassified  (Fig. 2)  . Each edit process addresses single edit request, such as move this concept to class t, and starts with fresh agent. Each request provides few support images labeled with the desired class (five for relabeling, eight for the fix tasks) and 64 reference images, labeled with the networks original predictions to indicate what should remain unchanged. The agent never sees the images themselves, and it observes only how the network responds to them. Within each edit process, the agent can iteratively inspect, modify, and evaluate the network. It inspects predictions, layer activations, feature contributions to logits, and parameter values. It then modifies weights by setting, adding to, or scaling individual entries, rows, channels, or whole tensors, anywhere in the classification head or the backbone. The protocol does not restrict which parameters are changed or how, the only limits are the number of calls and the size of single edit call. During the process, the agent can probe the modified network on the provided images, revise its changes, undo the last edit, or reset the weights. The agent submits these tool calls through model responses, which can contain several of these calls. Each edit process is limited to 20 forward probes, 30 weight reads, and 8 edit calls. single edit call may change up to 65,536 parameters, and single read returns at most 512 values. This write parameter budget is enough to rewrite the entire head of every network in one call (the largest, ResNet-50 on Entity-30, has 61,470 parameters) and any row, channel, bias or normalization layer of the backbone. At the same time, the read parameter budget, stops the agent from exfiltrating and retraining the network. Undo and reset do not count towards the edit budget, and do not restore it either. During editing, the agent further sees only an anonymous request ID, never receives images from the test set, and has no information about how the network was trained. Its system prompt encourages targeted edits that generalize beyond the provided examples (full text in Sec. A.3). An edit process ends when the agent submits its modified weights. If the agent stops without submitting or reaches the limit of 150 model responses, the original weights are evaluated. 3.2. Edit-Ready Training Standard training minimizes the cross-entropy LCE on the training labels and does not enforce editability. Edit-Ready Training (ERT) in contrast rehearses during training the edits that LLM agents make. To enable an agent to edit any parameter of the head or the backbone, our editing protocol does not constrain these edits during weight-space programming. However, during training the rehearsed edits are meant to simulate real Opus edits. Therefore, during small prestudy, we have tasked Opus to edit ERM-trained networks. We found that Opus mainly (>90%) changes head weights, an observation which we could also confirm later during our full edit analysis (see Sec. 5.3). Furthermore, the performed edits were mostly in rank-one manner, i.e., confined to the rows of the source and the target class, and concentrated on the few features that differ most between the support and the reference images. To simulate such edits during training, each training step draws few edit episodes that simulate an edit request to move concept of class to target class t. During these episodes, four support images of define the edit, four unseen query images of check that it generalizes, and reference images of other concepts from the batch check that their predictions stay unchanged. Edit episodes draw only from training concepts, concepts that editors later changed during testing are never used. During the training process, all edit episodes pass through the three ERT steps (see Fig. 1 (a)), which we describe below. Edit simulation. The extra cost per training step are the forward and backward passes over the episode images, which are appended to the training batch, and one closed-form edit per episode. 4. Experimental Setup 4.1. Network Training Vision model training. All networks to be edited are initialized with ImageNet weights and are classificationfine-tuned on the datasets classes: ResNet-18 [12] and ViT-B/16 [6] on Waterbirds (100 epochs), CIFAR-100 (30 epochs) and PACS (50 epochs), and ResNet-50 on Entity-30 (20 epochs). Since training compute and frontier model requests are limited, we train single network per training method and setting, with the exception of multiple trained networks for the seed ablation in Sec. 5.2. The intervals we report therefore reflect variation across edit processes, conditional on the trained networks. The seed ablation in Sec. 5.2 supports this design: the variation between networks trained with different seeds is negligible compared to the variation between edit processes on the same network. Baselines. We compare our ERT against three baselines. Standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) minimizes cross-entropy only. Label smoothing (LS) replaces the onehot target with 0.8 on the true class and 0.2 spread over all classes [38], to obtain less peaked logits [25] such that small change can move decision. ENN denotes Editable Neural Networks [36]. ENN is analogous to ERT, but simulates the edit with one or five gradient steps on the support 4 Figure 2. Two image types are used during editing. Support images carry the class they should receive after the edit (concept to relabel, errors to correct). Reference images are samples whose predictions must stay as they are. images, = ηW ES CE(W (x) + b, t). While the original ENN paper allows for arbitrary edit locations, we choose the head parameters, as these were mainly edited by LLM editors in our pre-study (see Sec. 3.2). Like ERT, ENN backpropagates the post-edit losses into all weights. LS and ENN were the strongest alternatives to standard training in pool of ten methods, which we have filtered using scripted edits resembling real LLM edits. Other techniques in the pool included sharpness-aware minimization [9], dropout [37], auxiliary concept labels [18] and sparse final layer [41] (details in Sec. B.2). Hyperparameter tuning. ERT, as well as all baseline methods, were hyperparameter tuned with the same protocol on two ResNet-18 settings: Waterbirds and CIFAR100. To keep compute needs low and the number of frontier model requests manageable, we also used scripted edits for selection. Furthermore, the ViT models reuse the ResNet18 tuned hyperparameters, and PACS and Entity-30 reuse the CIFAR-100 tuned hyperparameters, across all methods. Search spaces and selected values can be found in Sec. B.1. 4.2. Weight-Space Programming Editing tasks. We evaluate on three kinds of edit requests (see Fig. 2). Relabel concept: fine-grained concept moves to another class. The concept is bird species on Waterbirds [30] (two classes) or fine class on CIFAR-100 [19] (20 superclasses). Fix confusion (CIFAR-100, and Entity30 [32], 30-class subset of ImageNet [5]): superclass is wrongly predicted as B, which should be corrected. Fix subgroup (PACS [20]): misclassified sketches of one class should be corrected. LLM editors and protocol. The two main editors are GPT6 Astra (high reasoning effort) and Claude Opus 5.5 (default effort), each restricted to the WeightLab tools. Both cover all nine settings with all training methods. Three open-weight editors test how far the results carry over to weaker models: GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Gemma-4-26B (detailed numbers in Sec. E). Each editor handles eight edit requests per setting and training method, each with its own images, on one trained network, or split over two networks on PACS and three on the Entity-30 confusion fix (three requests each), which the seed ablation in Sec. 5.2 uses. We pair results of the same editor for different training methods and compare two training methods with an exact two-sided sign-flip test on the paired differences. The main grid contains 292 scored edit processes of Astra, 308 of Opus and 757 of the three open-weight editors. Including ablations and pilots, the five editors made more than 2,600 scored edit processes with more than 75,000 tool calls, and the median edit process takes about three minutes for Astra and Opus (Sec. H). Metrics. The reported scores are computed on held-out test images that no editor sees. For relabeling, success is the fraction of test images of the concept predicted as t, and the side effect is the fraction of test images of all other concepts whose prediction flips. For the two fix tasks, success is the fraction of the targeted test errors that the edit corrects, and the side effect is the fraction of originally correct test images outside the target group that become wrong. The net score as our primary measure reports success minus side effect, as also reported by Sinitsin et al. [36]. 5. Results 5.1. Main Results Baseline comparison. Tab. 1 shows the net scores of the two main editors (details on open-weight editors are found in Sec. E). ERT has the highest mean net score for both editors (Astra: 0.74, against 0.71 for ENN, 0.63 for LS and 0.63 for ERM; Opus: 0.72, against 0.68, 0.65 and 0.60). ERTs gain over ERM is +0.12 for both (p < 0.001 over the paired edit processes), and for Opus it is the only gain that stays significant when each of the nine settings counts as one observation (p = 0.047; ENN = 0.17), as each method helps strongly on only few settings. Ablations We have run four main ablations to investigate ERTs dependence on type, location and number of edits, as well as seed used during training. Edit rule ablation. To obtain insights on the effect of edit rules used during training, we retrained ERT on Waterbirds with ResNet-18 with seven edit variants: more units, larger steps, bias shift or sparse edits of the size of Opuss own (see Sec. 5.3), ENNs gradient step as additional rule, and stronger rehearsal. No variant differs reliably from the reference for Opus (differences from 0.06 to +0.06, none significant), and stronger rehearsal, trained for eight of the nine settings (all but the Entity-30 confusion fix), is ahead in three and behind in five. The benefit of ERT thus does not seem to depend on matching the editors edit closely (details in Sec. F.1). Backbone edit ablation. All of the tested rules edit only the final layer, whereas Opus sometimes also edits the backbone (see Fig. 3). To investigate if ERT should facilitate also backbone edits, we retrained modified ERT on Waterbirds with ResNet-18, where most backbone edits occur. During this training we introduced third rule: lower the input of the last ReLU on the selected channels, the backbone edit Opus makes most often on ERM trained networks. While the network keeps its accuracy (92.6% against 92.9%) under this edit, Opus does not profit: its net score is 0.61 against 0. below show that this shape holds for all tasks, architectures and training methods. of 16 on ENN and 1 of 16 on ERT networks. Edit progression. To obtain insights on the progress during an edit process, we rebuilt the weights after every edit call from the logged tool calls and scored them like submission (all 308 edit processes of Opus and 292 of Astra). Both editors reach most of their final net score with the first edit, which also costs the most accuracy on the full test sets (about 10 points for Opus, 5 to 10 for Astra). The later edits repair substantial share of this side effect (see Fig. 5). Astra trades some success for fewer side effects after the first edit (ERT from 0.77 to 0.73, ERM from 0.69 to 0.63), whereas Opus passes through clearly worse intermediate states (0.50 to 0.58) before it recovers. ERT is ahead of ERM after every edit, by 0.04 to 0.13 for Opus and 0.03 to 0.12 for Astra, so the comparison does not depend on when an edit process is stopped. For all training methods, accuracy on the full test sets still ends 3 to 4 points below the unedited network after the final edit. Even with frontier LLMs, targeted edits by weightspace programming thus still can cost overall accuracy. Edit locations. Fig. 3 shows what the edit processes behind Tab. 1 change. Both editors almost always edit the final layer: Astra changes its weights in 291 of 292 edit processes and Opus in 296 of 308, in 151 and 199 of them together with its bias. Edits to the backbone are rare, 4 edit processes of Astra and 14 of Opus, and all but one of them change the batch-norm bias before the last ReLU of ResNet-18. For Opus they concentrate on Waterbirds with ResNet-18 (12 of 48 edit processes, against 2 of 260 elsewhere), and on networks that were not prepared for editing: 5 of 8 edit processes on ERM networks and 2 of 8 with LS, against 4 Figure 5. Progress per edit. Net score (upper curves) and change in test accuracy (lower curves, as fraction) after each of the 8 edit calls, averaged over the nine settings and all edit processes of Tab. 1. Bands show 1 standard error. 8 Edit shapes. In every task, dataset and architecture, Opuss change to the final layer is rank one (median share of its energy in the first singular value above 99% in every setting), confined to the rows of the source and the target class, and sparse (median 11 to 64 feature columns, 28% of the features). The columns are chosen by contrast. Of the eight features that differ most between the concept and the reference images, the edit contains 3.2 to 4.5, against 0.1 to 1.4 by chance. The training method does not seem to change this shape. Among closed-form edits computed from the same support images, the closest to Opuss edits, on the entries it changed, is rank-one re-route along the contrast, ERTs direction rule without removal (mean cosine 0.72 to 0.93 on eight of the nine settings), followed by gradient step, the edit ENN rehearses (0.51 to 0.87); on the Entity-30 confusion fix, neither is close (0.38 and 0.40). An LLM that edits by hand thus arrives at sparse version of the edits that both edit-aware methods rehearse, and how gradient-like an edit is does not seem to predict which method wins. Method differences. What differs between training methods is the size of the edit. On Waterbirds with ResNet-18, Opuss change to the classifier weights is about five times larger on ERM-trained networks than on prepared ones (median ℓ2 norm 7.5, against 1.4 for ERT and 1.6 for ENN), with similar number of changed units. Preparation thus does not change what kind of edit Opus makes, as it makes small, ordinary edit sufficient where an ERM-trained network needs large one or an edit inside the backbone. 6. Conclusion and Future Work We presented the first systematic study of weight-space programming for vision models, with benchmark of LLM agents that edit trained classifiers and with Edit-Ready Training (ERT), which rehearses the head edits these agents write. Over more than 2,600 scored edit processes, ERT has the highest mean net score for both GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Further, standard networks already support targeted edits in easy settings, and preparation pays off where they resist. Our study also leaves several directions open. It covers image classification with three backbones and four datasets. Other vision tasks, larger backbones and generative models remain to be tested. With 8 to 16 paired edit processes per cell, only large differences between methods are detectable. Hyperparameters were tuned and baselines selected with scripted editors on ResNet-18 rather than with agents. Finally, with every training method, edits still lower test accuracy. Preparation that also preserves accuracy, rehearsal of edits inside the backbone or tailored to specific editor, and sequences of edits to one network are natural next steps. We release all tasks, trajectories and scores so that new methods and editors can be compared directly.

System prompt All five editors receive the same system prompt for every edit process, independent of task, dataset, backbone and training method: System prompt all editors, all edit processes You are careful model-editing engineer. You are given the ID of one editing task. Your job is to improve trained neural network by directly editing its existing weights, using only the weightlab tools. Rules: Use only the weightlab tools. Start with open_task(task_id) and read the objective and budget carefully. You can only run the model forward on the provided support examples (probes), read weights, and apply direct weight edits.
